newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COFFEE--Domestic prices seen up as export tax ends.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE--Domestic prices seen up as export tax ends.

text.p: Senate approval of a bill removing a 13 pct export tax brought optimism to exporters but caution to roasters who fear an increase in domestic prices.
"We expect exports in October, November and December to be higher," said Joaquim Libanio Leite, spokesman for Brazilian export group Abecafe.

"We have to see how the market works as of now. If there is not enough coffee, prices will rise (for domestic roasters)," said Americo Sato, president of Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry (ABIC).
On September 12, the Senate approved a bill making exports of primary commodities and some semi-manufactured goods exempt from the so-called ICMS export tax.

The bill is expected to take effect September 16 after President Fernando Henrique Cardoso signs the law. The Planning Ministry estimates exports to grow between six and 12 percent as a result of the measure. It noted the impact on exports would be equivalent of a seven percent devaluation.
Exporters expect the new legislation to help increasing sales at a time Brazilian exports are usually higher due to the ongoing harvest.
In August, Brazil exported 1.54 million coffee bags, the largest volume of the year.
"The bill will boost even more our exports, helping us to meet our commitment at the ACPC," said Manoel Bertone, grower's representative.

Under the ACPC retention plan, Brazil's export quotas total 15 million 60-kg bags in which nine million bags should be exported between July and December and six million bags from January through June 1997.
But higher exports in upcoming months, analysts said, could trigger an increase in domestic prices for roasters.

Analysts said the 1996/1997 crop, which is estimated to be 24.5 million 60-kg bags, will not be enough to meet ACPC export commitments of 15 million and domestic demand of nearly 14 million by roasters and the soluble industry.

In addition, the elimination of the 13 percent export tax is likely to trigger a dispute among exporters and growers on prices. Analysts said exporters will back a drop in prices while producers want prices to rise.
Mario Malta, spokesman for the Brazil's Soluble Industry Association (ABICS), said growers and exporters are likely to share the benefits of the tax exemption.

"Domestic prices will rise and international prices will fall. Due to that, the domestic industry will have to acquire coffee at a higher price while international firms will have cheaper coffee," Malta said. He noted the Brazilian soluble coffee could lose competitiveness abroad.
"If prices rise too much, we expect the government to sell coffee from its stocks," said Americo Sato.
Earlier this year, the government has agreed to hold monthly auctions until December of up to 200,000 60-kg bags for the sector.
In the domestic market Escritorio Carvalhaes on September 12 quoted fine-to-extrafine Mogiana Minas green beans at 117/118 reais per 60 kg.
On the export market, Santos brokers Wolthers & Associates quoted specialty 17/18s at 15 over New York for October shippment, unchanged from last week.
Fine 17/18s was quoted at two under and Swedish qualities were flat at nine under.
-- Sao Paulo newsroom, 55-11-2324411.
